title.narrative: Intelligence and Security Sector Reform Programme in North Macedonia (2021 - 2026)

description.narrative: By building on recent achievements during Phase I (2017-2021), the objective of this programme is to continue a process of democratic reforms within the security sector in North Macedonia, by working closely with national partners to operationalize and make sustainable initial results made, aimed at creating a more accountable and through that ultimately a more effectively governed security and intelligence sector.

Partners and beneficiaries in North Macedonia:•Cabinet of the President (National Security Advisor); •The Parliament; •Prime Minister’s Office; •Ministry of Interior;•Law Enforcement agencies; •Ministry of Defense; •Ministry of Justice;•Security and Intelligence Services (the so-called authorised bodies);•Operational Technical Agency (OTA); •Agency for Personal Data Protection; •Directorate for Security of Classified Information; •Academy for Judges and Public Prosecutors; •State Public Prosecutor Office for Organised Crime and Corruption; •Other courts and judicial institutions; •Ombudsperson; •State Audit Office;•Commission for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information;•State Administrative Inspectorate;•Various CSOs and media outlets.

The proposed programme intervention supports Macedonian reform areas outlined in the Plan 2018, aiming at a comprehensive security, justice and intelligence sector reform. It further supports the Macedonian Defence Strategy in having the different intelligence service providers and their oversight institutions acting in accordance with Euro-Atlantic standards. Other governmental strategies’ implementation which this programme explicitly supports are the Transparency Strategy of the Government of the Republic of North Macedonia (2019-2021), the Open Data Strategy (2018-2021) , and the Communication Strategy 2019/2020 , all aiming at increasing transparency, outreach and public access to governmental activities, thus building public trust in their leadership.

Working together with national partners to align the legal and institutional framework of the intelligence and security sector with relevant Euro-Atlantic principles and good practice and respect of human rights (Outcome 1); improving existing capacity of external oversight bodies to conduct effective and transparent oversight and control (Outcome 2); and helping ensure the public is informed on the functionality and results of the intelligence and security accountability system (Outcome 3);, the DCAF intervention strategy aims to ensure that intelligence and security services in North Macedonia function effectively under active democratic control and oversight and fight serious and organised crime and curb corruption in line with good practice of accountability and respect for human rights (Project goal). Ultimately, the Programme seeks to make an effective and sustainable contribution towards improved democratic governance of the intelligence and security (law enforcement) sector thus contributing to enhanced accountability, stability, rule of law and security for the state and the citizens (Development Goal)

title.narrative: Annual Report 2023 - Narrative

comment.narrative: Annual reporting by intelligence and security sector institutions and oversight actors is not sufficiently comprehensive, appropriate, and transparent.

•Four in-depth stories/mini-TV documentaries (eight to 12 minutes each), 1 interview with OTA Director and 1 interview with the Minister of Interior on topics related to intelligence and security sector reform aired as part of the “360 Degrees” TV show on Macedonian Radio-television (MRT). These mini documentaries were also shared and extensively promoted on the website, Facebook page, and YouTube channel of 360 Degrees, as well on DCAF’s official website, social media and YouTube channel. They helped increase the Programme’s visibility and informed the broader public on the progress of reforms in the intelligence and security sector. The mini-documentaries attracted significant viewership and engagement, with each video receiving more than 35.000 - views on TV . The total viewership of the videos is 161,000 views on TV, and 5,287 views on Facebook.•Three Gender Talks (moderated discussions) were organised in cooperation with partner CSO UNI-FORM with interlocutors from intelligence agencies, MoI and MoD. Each Gender Talk was attended by more than 30 participants (representatives of the intelligence and security institutions and representatives of CSOs and media organizations/outlets).•14 representatives from CSOs and media were trained throughout 2023 to contribute to the informal civilian oversight and for better-informed public debate. Guidelines for Informal Civilian•Oversight of Intelligence and Security conducted by CSOs and Media in North Macedonia was developed as a joint product.

title.narrative: 3.3: Transparency, towards the public is improved for the overall work of the intelligence and law enforcement actors, respecting the limits of classified information and personal data protection (GDPR).

comment.narrative: Annual reporting by intelligence and security sector institutions and oversight actors is not sufficiently comprehensive, appropriate, and transparent.

•Four theoretical and practical trainings on report drafting were organised with intelligence and security sector institutions. The trainings resulted in the development of the Guide for Developing Annual Reports in Security and Intelligence Services and Control and Oversight Institutions in North Macedonia. Drawing upon the guidelines outlined in the Guide and adhering to the legally mandated obligations, the Operational Technical Agency (OTA) thoroughly crafted its annual report for the year 2023, subsequently presenting it to the Parliament for review and consideration.

title.narrative: 2.1: Quality and frequency of direct oversight interaction between the Parliament and intelligence services increased to meet oversight effectiveness.

comment.narrative: Cooperation between the Parliament and security and intelligence services exists but does not meet full oversight needs.

Most of the MPs (members of the 3 parliamentary committees supervising the security and intelligence sectors, representatives of all political parties), as well as the parliamentary staff that support the three oversight committees, participated in capacity building activities (trainings, workshops, working visits, awareness activities) organized by DCAF throughout 2023 (this process started since 2021). Notably, half of the participants were women. MPs and parliamentary staffers involved in the capacity building activities noted an increase in their awareness and comprehension of security and intelligence governance, accountability, and oversight and increase in confidence for conducting oversight activities. The parliamentary oversight process over the intelligence and security enhanced in both quality and frequency. In 2023, the three parliamentary committees overseeing security and intelligence conducted 8 main oversight activities. Namely, these activities include reports, 6 oversight hearings, and _2 oversight visits to the National Security Agency (NSA) and Intelligence Agency (IA). During the period spanning from May 17 to June 15, 2023, the Committee for Oversight of the Implementation of Measures for Interception of Communications conducted 6 classified oversight sessions and hearings, focusing on scrutinizing the operations of the Operational Technical Agency (OTA). Subsequently, the Committee publicly disclosed its consensual conclusion through a press conference and forwarded its findings to the Public Prosecution for further investigation. Additionally, informal channels such as coordination and ad hoc meetings are enhancing cooperation between intelligence agencies and committees, signifying progress towards more effective oversight.

title.narrative: 2.2: Increased consistency of judicial practice (prosecutors and judges) in authorization and review of intrusive methods (intrusive methods to be based on law, be non-discriminatory, have a legitimate aim, and be a “necessary” and “proportional” response).

comment.narrative: The ECHR case law is not regularly observed by prosecutors and judges in the request and authorisation of intrusive methods. The judicial practice (interpretation and application of law by prosecutors and judges) in authorization of intrusive methods is still not consistent and adequate.

The reports from the Public Prosecutor’s Office in 2022 indicate there was a reduction in the number of cases where special investigative measures were implemented compared to 2021, decreasing from 59 to 53 cases. In general, the intrusive measures applied by the Public Prosecutor's Office are reducing each year (specifically the number of wiretaps, physically monitored persons, deployment of persons with concealed identity to detect more serious forms of crimes).•Draft Guidelines for the Destruction of Data Produced by SIMs was developed throughout 2023 with a working group consisting of judicial practitioners and experts. The Guidelines are currently in the process of being verified by judicial sector stakeholders.Trainers from Academy for Judges and Public Prosecutors applied skills gained from DCAF’s capacity building to deliver 5 trainings on the Implementation of measures for the interception of communications and 13 trainings on other various topics – organised crime/corruption, financial crime, custody, ethics, hate crime, and confiscation – throughout 2022 and 2023.•Collection of Case-Law on SIMs in North Macedonia developed throughout 2023. It is expected to be made available in 2024 on the Academy’s website in local languages for use by the students and practitioners.

title.narrative: 2.5: Recommendations from the GSA process translated into Gender Action Plan with the capacity to be configured as a complementary part of the institutional gender activities, plans and strategies of the MoD.

comment.narrative: The Ministry of Defense and Army do not have a Gender Action Plan based on a thorough institutional assessment.

•The Gender Self-Assessment of the MoD is finalised, and the end-products (GSA Report and Gender Action Plan) are drafted (following data collection and analysis phase in 2023). Final endorsement is expected by the Minister in April 2024.•13 members of the MoD working group and the Coordinator of Equal Opportunities were trained on gender assessment methodology.

title.narrative: 1.3: All missing requirements and standards, for automated exchange of biometric (DNA) data pursuant to the PCC Prüm Agreement are in place and are sufficient for exchange.

comment.narrative: The Ministry of Interior has established a solid normative base in the field of DNA exchange, however not yet sufficient to initiate automated exchange of such data, pursuant to the PCC Prüm Agreement.

Internal guidelines and manuals for DNA profiling and analysis necessary for the automated exchange of DNA data were developed in 2023 (including Guidelines and Strategy for Recovering Biological Samples for DNA and Interpretation Guideline for Autosomal STR Profiling).

title.narrative: 2.3: The Ministry of Interior of North Macedonia (MoI) has strategic and operational capacity to effectively build integrity in line with European values and good policing practice, enabling more effective oversight.

comment.narrative: The Section for Internal Control, Criminal Investigations, and Professional Standards (DICCIPS), in cooperation with DCAF, developed an Integrity Plan over the past three years. The Plan assesses the corruption risk of all job positions in the Ministry of Interior, in accordance with the Rulebook on systematization of job positions in the MoI, proposing measures aimed to reduce risk.

The MoI implemented the first year of its Integrity Plan (2023 – 2025) and produced an annual report that indicates an implementation rate of 100%, with all trainings, controls, and other activities performed.

title.narrative: 1.2: The MoI is acting in accordance with new amendments to the law on Internal Affairs and in accordance with the MoI Integrity Plan.

comment.narrative: The amendments to the Law on Internal Affairs, which are currently in parliamentary procedure (June 2021), make a change in Article 66 of the law that sets up the general criteria a person should meet so that he/she can be employed in the MoI, with a new criterion being introduced – the person must pass an Integrity Test carried out by the MoI. A professional integrity test will also be conducted for existing employees, contributing to the prevention of corruption and abuse of office, aimed at strengthening the integrity of Ministry and Police employees and preventive action.

The Integrity Plan and Action Plan (2023-2025) of the MoI was developed by the MoI’s WG on Integrity. It was endorsed and adopted by MoI leadership in 2023 and was made publicly available on the MoI’s website. It will assist the MoI to prevent and mitigate corruption risks in its institution.

title.narrative: 1.1 (a) Amended laws, bi-laws and procedures on intelligence aligned with international principles, gender and human rights obligations, good practice and respecting the diversity of the citizens of the Republic of North Macedonia, adopted by Parliament.

comment.narrative: The current law, by-laws and procedures are not suitable to allow for effective oversight of the intelligence services. In addition, legally mandated oversight bodies are functioning but not sufficiently effective. The formal relationship between the Parliament and the Council for Civilian Supervision remains inadequate as a result.

Amendment of the Law on Interception of Communications (LIC) was passed by the Parliament on 18 July 2023 with a 2/3rds majority. The adoption of the LIC amendment provides a legal foundation for the proper functioning of the Council for Civilian Supervision (CCS) and Parliament’s engagement of technical experts to support the Council.

Security operating procedures for Shielded Room were drafted and finalised in 2023 through an inclusive process with the Parliament, the Directorate for Security of Classified Information (DSCI), and the MoI. This is one of the documents needed for the accreditation of the Shielded Room. The Statement for Security Needs and Security Assessment were also developed in 2023.

Security operating procedures for Shielded Room were drafted and finalised in 2023 through an inclusive process with the Parliament, the Directorate for Security of Classified Information (DSCI), and the MoI. This is one of the documents needed for the accreditation of the Shielded Room. The Statement for Security Needs and Security Assessment were also developed in 2023.

The Committee on Oversight of Implementation of Measures for Interception of Communication has developed and adopted its Rules of Procedure (R&P), based on the Parliament’s R&P and the provisions from the LIC that regulate oversight.

title.narrative: 3.1: Public can debate and challenge the content of reports produced by intelligence and law enforcement actors.

comment.narrative: The intelligence sector reforms and accountability are not sufficiently and publicly debated and professionally addressed by media and CSOs.

The event was additionally livestreamed via an MIA (Media Information Agency) media aggregator and was summarised in a short documentary video produced by 360 Stepeni. This media attention would suggest that media interest and resultingly public interest in the topic of oversight has grown.

comment.narrative: Annual reporting by intelligence and security sector institutions and oversight actors is not sufficiently comprehensive, appropriate, and transparent.

Guide for Developing Annual Reports in Security and Intelligence Services and Control and Oversight Institutions was developed through a series of multi-stakeholder workshops with 18 public institutions participating. It aims to improve the reporting standards within the institutions and was internally shared within the intelligence and security institutions and has been endorsed by intelligence leadership as a valuable and effective tool. OTA has already started using the guidelines when preparing their annual reports.

Security sector institutions and intelligence agencies have demonstrated a consistent commitment to transparency, as reflected in their active participation in DCAF events, including Gender Talks and interviews for mini documentaries. A monitoring report conducted with CSOs and the media training group revealed that the gap between civil society and state institutions is shrinking, as evidenced by increased access to Ministers and Directors of intelligence and security sector institutions—previously less attainable for interviews and meetings.

The Forensics Department published the Brochure/Service Catalogue on Forensics Services. It serves as an informative tool for justice institutions to get more information on valuable forensics services.

title.narrative: Indicator #3.2: Media coverage and CSO research paper mentioning the topic of intelligence reform, integrity and accountability

comment.narrative: Annual reporting by intelligence and security sector institutions and oversight actors is not sufficiently comprehensive, appropriate, and transparent.

The Ceremonial Opening of the Shielded Room and Protected Workplace in the Parliament was covered by a range of local mainstream media (TV channels, newspapers, and media portals). In addition, there was significant engagement on social media (via Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn) with content shared/re-shared and tweeted/re-tweeted on DCAF’s and participants’ social media profiles, including the ones of policymakers. The event was additionally summarised in two short documentaries produced by 360 Degrees and the Parliamentary Channel. This extensive coverage indicates significant public attention and interest in the topic of oversight.

There is an increase in reporting on intelligence and security matters by the CSO and media group that attends the trainings for civilian oversight. For instance, TELMA TV produced 45-minute video documentary examining the announced merger of the Intelligence Agency and the National Security Agency (NSA) into a single entity. The same TV channel also broadcasted series of reports (well-informed videos) on the controversial election process of the members of the Council of Civilian Supervision. ALFA TV produced a compelling live broadcast episode addressing the potential merger of the Intelligence Agency (IA) and the National Security Agency (NSA).

Three in-depth stories/mini-TV documentaries (eight to 12 minutes each), related to intelligence and security sector reform aired as part of the “360 Degrees” TV show on Macedonian Radio-television (MRT). These mini documentaries were also shared and extensively promoted on the website, Facebook page, and YouTube channel of 360 Degrees, as well on DCAF’s official website, social media and YouTube channel. They helped increase the Programme’s visibility and informed the broader public on the progress of reforms in the intelligence and security sector. The mini documentaries attracted significant viewership and engagement, with each video receiving more than 1K views on both YouTube and Facebook.

title.narrative: Indicator # 2.1: Quality and frequency of direct oversight interaction between the Parliament and intelligence services increased to meet oversight effectiveness.

comment.narrative: Cooperation between the Parliament and security and intelligence services exists but does not meet full oversight needs.

After the consolidation of the new Parliament following the 2024 elections and the establishment of new Committees with revised compositions, three oversight-related activities were conducted. Four parliamentary staff members were trained in communication and advisory skills to support new MPs in the oversight process.

Shielded Room and Protected Workplace was constructed and established in the Parliament. The Parliament is equipped with secure facility and protective systems for handling sensitive data and confidential information during the oversight activities.

title.narrative: Indicator #2.2: Increased consistency of judicial practice (prosecutors and judges) in authorization and review of intrusive methods (intrusive methods to be based on law, be non-discriminatory, have a legitimate aim, and be a “necessary” and “proportional” response)

comment.narrative: The ECHR case law is not regularly observed by prosecutors and judges in the request and authorisation of intrusive methods. The judicial practice (interpretation and application of law by prosecutors and judges) in authorization of intrusive methods is still not consistent and adequate.

Collection of Case-Law on SIMs in North Macedonia was developed throughout 2023 and 2024. It was made available on the Academy’s website in local languages for use by the students and practitioners as additional educational tool and useful resource material. The case law will assist current and future judges and prosecutors to act in a consistent manner when resorting to the use of SIMs.

The reports from the Public Prosecutor’s Office in 2023 indicate there was an increase in cases where special investigative measures (SIM) were implemented compared to previous years that showcased consistent decline. However, despite this increase, the number of individuals with established identities subjected to these measures saw only a slight uptick. Regarding criminal cases covered by special investigative measures, there is a decrease in the number from 136 in 2022 to 93 in 2023.

Trainers from the Academy for Judges and Public Prosecutors (AJPP) utilized the skills gained from DCAF's capacity-building programs to deliver 22 academic hours of training on the implementation of measures for the interception of communications, along with 5 additional sessions on topics including organized crime, corruption, financial crime, custody, ethics, hate crime, and confiscation throughout 2024. The Benchbook has been distributed to all 97 students of the AJPP's future judges and public prosecutors.

title.narrative: Indicator #2.5: Recommendations from the GSA process translated into Gender Action Plan with the capacity to be configured as a complementary part of the institutional gender activities, plans and strategies of the MoD

comment.narrative: The Ministry of Defense and Army do not have a Gender Action Plan based on a thorough institutional assessment.

A new MoD working group, comprising 16 administrative personnel from MoD, along with civilian and military staff from the Army (10 women and 6 men), has been established to implement and monitor the implementation of the Gender Action Plan (2024–2028).

A new systematization has been established in the MoD and the Army, which contributes to strengthening the gender structure in the MoD and the Army as outlined in the Gender Action Plan. This includes a minimum of three positions dedicated to gender equality within the MoD's Support Sector and a designated Advisor for Gender Equality in the Cabinet of the General Staff.

The Gender Action Plan (2024-2028) was officially adopted. It is a strategic document, setting clear objectives, actions and practical steps to overcome identified barriers to gender mainstreaming and inclusivity in the MoD and Army of North Macedonia.

title.narrative: Indicator #1.3: All missing requirements and standards, for automated exchange of biometric (DNA) data pursuant to the PCC Prüm Agreement are in place and are sufficient for exchange.

comment.narrative: The Ministry of Interior has established a solid normative base in the field of DNA exchange, however not yet sufficient to initiate automated exchange of such data, pursuant to the PCC Prüm Agreement.

The Department for Forensic Examinations at the MoI has met all necessary legal, technical, and operational requirements and is fully prepared to initiate the international automated exchange of biometric data (DNA and dactyloscopy) under the PCC Prüm framework. From a technical perspective, the required firewall infrastructure (hardware) have been successfully established. Legally, internal guideline modifications have been made in accordance with the PCC Prüm framework.

title.narrative: Indicator #2.3: The Ministry of Interior of North Macedonia (MoI) has strategic and operational capacity to effectively build integrity in line with European values and good policing practice, enabling more effective oversight.

comment.narrative: The Section for Internal Control, Criminal Investigations, and Professional Standards (DICCIPS), in cooperation with DCAF, developed an Integrity Plan over the past three years. The Plan assesses the corruption risk of all job positions in the Ministry of Interior, in accordance with the Rulebook on systematization of job positions in the MoI, proposing measures aimed to reduce risk.

The second Annual Report was issued by MoI on the implementation of its Integrity Plan (2023 – 2025) which indicates 90% implementation rate, with all trainings, controls, and other activities performed. Additionally, over 40 police inspectors from the MoI’s Department for Internal Control, Criminal Investigations, and Professional Standards (DICCIPS) were trained to strengthen their criminal investigation capacities, in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs. In 2024, DICCIPS initiated investigations into 1,366 cases of alleged illegal, unprofessional, and unethical conduct, as well as abuse of official position, reflecting a 10.6% increase compared to the previous year.

title.narrative: Indicator #1.1 (b): Amended laws, by-laws and procedures on intelligence implemented by oversight sector actors.

comment.narrative: The current law, by-laws and procedures are not suitable to allow for effective oversight of the intelligence services. In addition, legally mandated oversight bodies are functioning but not sufficiently effective. The formal relationship between the Parliament and the Council for Civilian Supervision remains inadequate as a result.

Security operating procedures for Shielded Room that were drafted through an inclusive process with the Parliament, the Directorate for Security of Classified Information (DSCI), and the MoI, along with the Statement for Security Needs and Security Assessment were handed over to DSCI and based on these documents the Shielded Room was smoothly accredited in 2024. After the accreditation in 2024, these documents are put into practical usage.

The Committee on Oversight of the Implementation of Measures for Interception of Communications strengthened its regulatory framework by adopting Rules of Procedure, which incorporate the Common Minimum Standards (CMS) for Conducting Control and Oversight Visits in the Security and Intelligence Institutions of the Republic of North Macedonia.

The Guidelines for the Destruction of Data Collected through Special Investigative Measures (SIMs) were developed following an inclusive multi-stakeholder process with a working group consisting of judicial practitioners and experts and received broad approval across the judiciary.

title.narrative: Indicator #3.1: Public can debate and challenge the content of reports produced by intelligence and law enforcement actors.

comment.narrative: The intelligence sector reforms and accountability are not sufficiently and publicly debated and professionally addressed by media and CSOs.

14 representatives from CSOs and media that were trained throughout 2023, started a ToT programme in 2024 in order to continue disseminating the acquired knowledge among their peers, organizations and networks. Guidelines for Informal Civilian Oversight of Intelligence and Security conducted by CSOs and Media in North Macedonia was updated as a joint product to reflect the new realities.

Roadmap with Performance Indicators for Assessing Transparency, Accountability, and Effectiveness in the Intelligence and Security Sector of North Macedonia was published after a two-year development process led by a partner CSO, with input from oversight actors and intelligence institutions. This Roadmap reflects and summarizes the practical and instrumental findings based on evidence and qualitative primary data retrieved from interviews, open-ended questionnaires and nominal group discussions with representatives from the intelligence and security sector and independent actors. A video was prepared by partner media organization in 2024 to promote the roadmap. The roadmap was already used throughout 2024 during trainings with CSOs/media and parliamentary staff on how to use the indicators to monitor the work of the intelligence and security institutions. It will be widely promoted throughout 2025.

Three Gender Talks (moderated discussions) were organised (one in 2023 and two in 2024) in cooperation with partner CSO UNI-FORM with interlocutors from intelligence agencies, MoI and MoD. Each Gender Talk was attended by more than 30 participants (representatives of the intelligence and security institutions and representatives of CSOs and media organizations/outlets).

comment.narrative: Employees from the Ministry of Interior, e.g. the Section for Crime – Technical Analysis and Expertise, and the National Central Unit for Information Exchange, are not sufficiently equipped with knowledge to administer automated exchange of DNA data.
By the end of 2023, relevant employees from the Ministry of Interior received the necessary vocational trainings.

The training was attended by employees from DNA identification laboratories within the Forensics Department and was conducted by two international experts in forensic sciences and DNA and two experts from INTERPOL.

title.narrative: Indicator 2.5.1: Judicial practitioners receive training on judicial authorisation of SIM (more concretely on interception of communications), use of European legal standards and principles related to information collection.

comment.narrative: No training delivered by the Academy on SIM.

(1) In 2021, most of the judicial practitioners working on criminal cases will undergo in-service training.(2) Each year starting 2021 candidates for future judges and prosecutors selecting the subject on interception of communications, will undergo 9 academic classes.(3) Starting mid 2021 supplementary self-paced online courses, undertaken by future candidates, judges and prosecutors working on criminal investigative matters.

In support of strengthening the training curricula in the Judicial Academy, DCAF organised a Working Visit to Judicial Training Centres in Spain between 13-16 February 2023 on Exchanging Good Practices on Conceptualising and Organising Judicial Training: the Spanish and the Macedonian Models for 11 representatives of the North Macedonian Academy for Judges and Public Prosecutors. Macedonian representatives (judges, prosecutors, and the Academy’s secretariat) met their Spanish counterparts from the Judicial Training Center in Barcelona, the Periodic Training Service of the Judicial School and the Public Assistance Service in Madrid, and the General Judicial Council in Madrid. Discussions, facilitated by a team of senior experts from the Spanish institutions, provided participants valuable insight into the Spanish judicial system and its educational system. Macedonian practitioners were particularly attentive to the process of selecting students, the evaluation system, the selection of trainers and mentors, and the internship programmes.

title.narrative: Indicator 2.3.1: Shielded Room and protected workspace constructed in Parliament and equipment installed.

comment.narrative: The Parliament has no protected workspace and meeting facility to discuss and store classified information, impeding meaningful exchange of sensitive and classified information with security and intelligence services. Parliament, in Feb 2020, approved the establishment of the shielded room. Within its Phase I Programme DCAF allocated funds as a contribution towards the establishment of the Shielded Room and protected workplace. Due to Covid-19 the process was delayed throughout 2020.
By the end of 2021 the Parliament has a Shielded Room and protected space installed.

DCAF organised Two Workshops on Developing Accreditation Documents for the Shielded Room and Protected Workspace in the Parliament of the Republic of North Macedonia. The first workshop took place from 16-17 February 2023 in Veles. The second workshop, held from 22-24 March 2023 in Berovo, was focused on developing a Statement of Security Needs and included practical work aimed at aligning views on the scope and concept of the accreditation documents. These workshops are part of a series of six workshops, facilitated by a local expert. The process will continue until all accreditation documents are developed and deployed following the construction of the Shielded Room. The finalisation of the accrediation documents will allow the Shielded Room to function once constructed.
By the end of 2021 the Parliament has a Shielded Room and protected space Installed.
The sixth tendering process for the Shielded Room was successful. The Assembly selected a bidder and the construction of the Shielded Room will begin soon.

title.narrative: Indicator 1.2: The MoI is acting in accordance with new amendments to the law on Internal Affairs and in accordance with the MoI's Integrity Plan.

comment.narrative: The amendments to the Law on Internal Affairs, which are currently in parliamentary procedure (June 2021), make a change in Article 66 of the law that sets up the general criteria a person should meet so that he/she can be employed in the MoI, with a new criterion being introduced – the person must pass an Integrity Test carried out by the MoI. A professional integrity test will also be conducted for existing employees, contributing to the prevention of corruption and abuse of office, aimed at strengthening the integrity of Ministry and Police employees and preventive action.
By the end of the programme (2024) the MoI is successfully implementing the Integrity Plan.

The MoI approved the Integrity Plan and Action Plan (2023 - 2025) and published it on their website. This achievement came after the successful delivery of a series of mentoring sessions and workshops in the period that increased the capacities of the Department for Internal Control for integrity planning.

title.narrative: Indicator 3.2.1: Public institutions legally mandated to oversee or control intelligence services report on their activities.

comment.narrative: There is none or inconsistent public reporting by intelligence sector actors taking place.
By 2022 four theoretical and practical trainings on report drafting organised with all intelligence sector actors.

DCAF held the Second Multi-stakeholder Workshop on Reporting Standards for Security/Intelligence Services and Control/Oversight Institutions between 27-28 February 2023 in Veles. Representatives responsible for reporting, public relations, and inter-institutional cooperation from intelligence and security services and institutions with an oversight or control mandate attended the workshop. During the workshop, each institution presented their process of reporting and identified common features across institutions. In addition, the expert on classified information from Croatia shared experiences and good practices related to the classification, declassification, and overclassification of reports and triggered interesting discussion among participants about existing reporting challenges.

By the end of 2025, 70% of the female MPs and staffers have attended organised activities and actively participated.

DCAF continued to support parliamentary staff in enhancing and institutionalizing oversight of intelligence and security. After several targeted trainings and two workshops on Developing a Framework for Communication, Analytical, and Advisory Skills, DCAF organized several advanced-level workshops in October and November 2025 to further strengthen the knowledge transfer and communication skills of parliamentary staff to be able to provide effective support to MPs through advice and training. These workshops aimed to continuously strengthen the capacity of parliamentary staff to effectively analyse security-related information, provide strategic advice, and communicate oversight findings in a clear and compelling manner. These interactive sessions also prompted peer learning and cross-institutional exchange of practical experiences.This quarter, 75% of the female staffers have attended organised activities and actively participated.
By the end of 2025, 70% of the female MPs and staffers have attended organised activities and actively participated.

Furthermore, DCAF organized a Parliamentary Working Visit from 17 to 20 November 2025 in Berlin for a parliamentary delegation led by the Secretary General of the Macedonian Assembly. The visit aimed at deepening parliamentary staff’s understanding of Germany’s comprehensive and multi-layered intelligence oversight system and included exchanges with members of the Bundestag, advisors on intelligence oversight, the G10 Commission, and the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection. These discussions provided comparative insights into institutional design, governance, legislative frameworks, and practical oversight approaches. The visit supported the professional development of parliamentary officials and staff, helping them reflect on how German practices can inform and strengthen parliamentary oversight over intelligence and security in North Macedonia. Participants also had the opportunity to join an organized tour of the Bundestag.This quarter, 75% of the female staffers have attended organised activities and actively participated.

DCAF continued with the extensive Training of Trainers (ToT) programme designed for civil society organizations and media professionals. The seventh ToT session that took place between 30-31 October 2025 in Veles focused on visualization theories and techniques, especially how to effectively use presentation tools and to deliver clear and compelling messages. The eight and final ToT session, held between 26-27 December 2025 in Skopje, centred on the importance of training evaluation as a means to measure learning outcomes, behaviour change, and institutional impact. This training initiative aimed to empower civil society organizations and media professionals with advanced knowledge and skills to effectively disseminate information on security sector reform and governance across their organizations and networks, while further strengthening oversight and accountability mechanisms. In 2026, DCAF will engage these certified trainers as expert contributors to the postgraduate micro-qualification programme accredited at the University Goce Delčev - Štip thus ensuring continuity and sustainability of the initiative.This quarter, 2 capacity building activities were delivered to CSOs and Media.

DCAF continued to rely on multi-stakeholder workshops to build trust and institutional connectivity among oversight actors. The multi-stakeholder workshop “New Technologies and Oversight”, held between 3-5 December 2025 in Gevgelija, brought together MPs, representatives of civil society, the media, and the Ombudsperson’s office to explore how emerging and rapidly evolving technologies are reshaping the landscape of security governance and democratic oversight. The workshop examined the legal, political, and strategic implications of new technologies, the evolving landscape of digital and hybrid threats, and the challenges posed by mass surveillance, profiling, and data-driven decision-making. The participants discussed how different oversight actors can collaborate to safeguard fundamental rights, especially the right to privacy, and ensure that technological and AI innovations used by security institutions remain transparent, accountable, and democratically governed. In the upcoming period, DCAF will continue to use multi-stakeholder formats to strengthen dialogue and build durable networks among diverse oversight actors.This multi-stakeholder event had 44% female participation.
80% of invited institutions attend each multi-stakeholder event.

DCAF continued with the support of the intelligence agencies and in the past period has organized several multi-institutional workshops on classified information management. In November and December 2025, DCAF held several meetings with the multi-institutional working group tasked to develop comprehensive Classification Guidelines that will be applicable in all intelligence institutions. The guidelines will outline standardised classification criteria, normative framework, and effective internal mechanisms for oversight and verification across institutions. DCAF will continue with the discussions and guidelines development to achieve improved institutional security and accountability through consistent information sharing.All invited institutions attended the organised events.

title.narrative: OUTPUT 2.8 – MoI – DICCIPS integrity testing: Capacity building activities (trainings/study visits and expert support, technical equipment) provided to the “Section for Internal Control, Criminal Investigations and Professional Standards (DICCIPS)” to effectively implement the MoI Action Plan on police integrity and perform investigations.

comment.narrative: Over the last two years DCAF supported the MoI in the development and drafting of the Integrity Plan. Presently, the Integrity Plan is pending approval from the Minister of Interior. The Ministry of Interior (MoI) is amending the law on internal affairs to improve the internal control mechanisms that promote integrity. The new law will include integrity testing measures as a means of internal control, which will be applied to both current and future employees of the MoI. The MoI does not possess technical equipment to perform professional integrity testing, which will be a requirement in accordance to the new Law on Internal Affairs. In addition, the North Macedonian Police have revised their Code of Ethics in 2020.
By the end of 2025, 80% of DICCIPS employees report increasing their capacities for conducting criminal and disciplinary investigations.

DCAF provides continuous support to the MoI Department for Internal Control, Criminal Investigations and Professional Standards and implements targeted capacity-building initiatives in the area of criminal investigations focusing on strengthening the analytical and investigative competencies of Internal Control officers. In November and December 2025, DCAF organised two specialised trainings that aimed to enhance the Internal Control Department’s institutional and operational capacities for detecting, analysing, and documenting corruption and other criminal offences committed by police officers. The Training on Financial Investigations and Analysis was held from 6 to 7 November 2025 in Skopje and aimed to strengthen participants skills in tracing financial flows, identifying illicit enrichment, and improving inter-agency cooperation in financial crime investigations. The sessions offered practical application of learned skills through case studies, as participants made in-depth analysis of financial documentation, and traced assets acquired through illegal means in order to build a strong case against corrupted police officers. DCAF organised the second Training on Criminal Investigations of Crimes Committed by Police Officers for the Internal Control Department from 11 to 12 December 2025 in Skopje. This highly interactive training held with public prosecutors, judges, criminal investigators and a lawyer offered Internal Control Officers different perspectives into conducting criminal investigations against police officers and focused on enhancing evidence gathering, timely processes and cooperation with the prosecution while ensuring accountability and respect for human rights. The sessions included analysing trends of police misconduct, particularly excessive use of force, harassment, and evidence tempering, and joint discussions on preventive measures and sustaining lawful and ethical police behaviour. DCAF will continue delivering a multifaced format of trainings to the Internal Control Department to support their transparent efforts in promoting integrity in the police service.To further promote institutional accountability and integrity, on 9 and 10 December 2025, the Ministry of Interior hosted an official delegation from the Republic of Moldova National Public Security Inspectorate for a peer exchange on integrity, internal control, and good governance practices within the security sector. Supported by DCAF Skopje and Chisinau Offices, this working visit on police integrity aimed to facilitate professional dialogue, exchange of experiences, and sharing of practical approaches to strengthening integrity systems, internal oversight mechanisms, and accountability processes in law enforcement institutions.DCAF continuously provided guidance and sustainable support in all phases of implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of the MoI Integrity Plan 2023-2025, and aiming to assess the final year of its implementation, organized a workshop for drafting the 2025 Annual Progress Report on 29 December 2025 in Skopje. The workshop gathered a dedicated working group from the Internal Control Department which assumed full ownership of the drafting process and remains committed to embedding integrity as an institutional value. DCAF will support the working group in the development of the second Professional Integrity Plan of the Ministry for the next three years based on the goals, principles, and methodology applied during the development of the first Integrity Plan while ensuring the sustainability of the proposed anti-corruption measures.

DCAF finalised the research initiative to enhance transparency and accountability in the use of Special Investigative Measures (SIMs) following a series of workshops, focus groups, interviews and drafting sessions conducted in the past several months in cooperation with the Academy of Judges and Public Prosecutors (AJPP) and the judiciary group. On 21 October 2025 a coordination workshop with the judiciary group was held in Skopje to review the final text, findings and recommendations of the comprehensive analysis report titled ‘Application of Special Investigative Measures in the Republic of North Macedonia’. The workshop aimed to collect final comments and remarks, harmonize views, and revise any potentially overlooked elements before publication. On 25 December 2025, DCAF organised a coordination meeting with the judges to discuss lessons learned from the sustained research process, and plan for a promotion event in 2026. This research process, which is based on DCAF’s Methodology guidelines for systematic monitoring and evaluation of SIMs usage, will serve as a baseline to monitor progress and will help the AJPP conduct such bi-annual assessments on their own. DCAF will promote this systematised assessment with 16 recommendations for improvement of judicial practice at a roundtable discussion on how Special Investigative Measures are lawfully approved, implemented, and overseen within the judiciary.

DCAF continued with the activities that are part of the Gender Self-Assessment (GSA) process in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) and the Army of North Macedonia. The field research, officially started in May 2023 and will last until the end of September 2023, consisting of interviews with key leaders from the MoD and the Army, focus groups with MoD and Army personnel, and surveys. The research will be concluded with an in-depth analysis, conducted by experts and the MoD’s Working Group (WG), that will identify gaps and weaknesses in the MoD and Army’s structures regarding gender equality as well as opportunities and entry points for gender mainstreaming.The MoD’s WG, consisting of 13 military and civilian representatives of the Army and administrative staff of the MoD, continues to have significant responsibility during the GSA process, specifically collecting information and providing organisational support, thus ensuring local ownership over the process. DCAF will continue to support the process beyond the research and analysis phases, namely during the preparation of the Gender Action Plan that will translate the findings and recommendations on gender mainstreaming into practical actions.

DCAF organised the Final Meeting for the MoI Working Group (WG) to Incorporate the Recommendations Received by the Reviewers of the Manual for Criminal and Technical Registration and Identification of Persons and Unknown Corpses on 28 April 2023 in Skopje. At this meeting, the WG members finalised the procedures for the criminal and technical registration and identification of persons and unknown corpses according to best practice and revised the text according to recommendations and proposals provided by regional forensics’ experts. The Manual is developed in line with PCC Prüm requirements related to the storage, processing, and automated exchange of DNA, dactyloscopic data, and photos, as well as national regulations related to the work of the Police. Once the Manual has been approved within the MoI, it will be adopted by the Minister as a by-law and distributed to all forensics technicians in the country, who will be expected to align their working procedures with the new standards.

title.narrative: Indicator #2.8.1: SICPS’ employees have updated knowledge and skills to perform their duties related to preventing corruption and integrity violations more efficiently within the MoI.

comment.narrative: Baseline # 2.8.1 – 2.8.4: Over the last two years DCAF supported the MoI in the development and drafting of the Integrity Plan. Presently, the Integrity Plan is pending approval from the Minister of Interior. The Ministry of Interior (MoI) is amending the law on internal affairs to improve the internal control mechanisms that promote integrity. The new law will include integrity testing measures as a means of internal control, which will be applied to both current and future employees of the MoI. The MoI does not possess technical equipment to perform professional integrity testing, which will be a requirement in accordance to the new Law on Internal Affairs. In addition, the North Macedonian Police have revised their Code of Ethics in 2020.
Target # 2.8.1: By end of 2023 all employees within the SICPS have undergone integrity training.

Between 9 – 12 May 2023 in Skopje, DCAF organised a series of mentoring sessions and workshops aimed at enabling trainers from the MoI to develop hybrid training on integrity and integrate integrity into other training curricula. DCAF supports these trainers in cooperation with the OSCE Mission to Skopje, currently implementing a three-year project aimed at developing hybrid learning courses on a range of topics for MoI employees. Through the mentoring sessions, the four trainers tasked with developing the hybrid course on integrity became more familiar with the topic, agreed upon the course’s format and concept, and discussed integrating the hybrid course on integrity into existing training structures with relevant institutions (Police Training Centre, Internal Control Department). DCAF will continue to support the development of integrity curricula and the organisation of train-the-trainers to enable sustained delivery of hybrid integrity courses. The development of these hybrid courses is expected to conclude in mid-2024. Meanwhile, DCAF supports the MoI in conceptualising and developing police integrity training courses that need to be delivered to different target groups in the MoI, identified in the MoI’s Integrity Plan. In this regard, DCAF organised an Initial Meeting of the Working Group (WG) for Developing a Training Course on Police Integrity on 12 June 2023. The WG is led by the Department for Internal Control, Criminal Investigations, and Professional Standards. The course will be developed to support the implementation of the Integrity Plan of the MoI (2023-2025) and will target police officers in different organisational units of the Ministry identified as most vulnerable to corruption risks. The WG members agreed to start working on the training curricula, which will be submitted to the Minister of Interior for approval. DCAF will continue to support this WG by providing advice and mentoring and organising a Train-the-Trainers course to prepare them for the successful delivery of the integrity course.

title.narrative: Indicator #1.2: The MoI is acting in accordance with new amendments to the law on Internal Affairs and in accordance with the MoI Integrity Plan.

comment.narrative: Baseline #1.2: The amendments to the Law on Internal Affairs, which are currently in parliamentary procedure (June 2021), make a change in Article 66 of the law that sets up the general criteria a person should meet so that he/she can be employed in the MoI, with a new criterion being introduced – the person must pass an Integrity Test carried out by the MoI. A professional integrity test will also be conducted for existing employees, contributing to the prevention of corruption and abuse of office, aimed at strengthening the integrity of Ministry and Police employees and preventive action.
Target #1.2: By end of the programme (2024) the MoI (Section for Internal Control, Criminal Investigations and Professional Standards - SICPS) is successfully implementing the Integrity Plan.

On 26 June 2023 a Launching Event of the Integrity Plan of the Ministry of Interior (2023-2025) was organised. The Integrity Plan, available on the MoI’s webpage, serves as a strategic document aimed at building integrity and hindering corrupt practices in MoI structures and police in North Macedonia by identifying corruption risks and establishing mechanisms that minimise those risks. It was previously a classified document and the launching event marks the conclusion of the MoI's redevelopment of the Plan as a public document. The MoI’s Department for Internal Control, Criminal Investigations, and Professional Standards developed the Plan in cooperation with DCAF, additionally consulting all organisational units of the MoI during development. This Plan is crucial for building public confidence in the MoI, contributing to regional stability, and ensuring North Macedonia’s compliance with EU standards. DCAF will continue to support the MoI to implement, monitor, and evaluate the Plan.

title.narrative: Indicator #1.4.2: Inter-institutional Protocols, harmonised Templates and Guidelines for different stages of SIM approval are drafted and submitted for approval by relevant institutions within the criminal justice chain.

comment.narrative: Baseline #1.4.1 - 1.4.2: Courts and prosecutorial offices have different (sometimes dated, or even contradictory) procedures and templates used in the authorisation of SIM. Harmonisation of practice and exchange of information are not in place to ensure effective authorisation of SIM, in agreement with new legislative provisions and European standards.
Target #1.4.2: By 2022 working groups draft proposals designed to unify and harmonise practice.

Upon the request of the Criminal Court in Skopje, DCAF organised the First Workshop on Conceptualising Procedures for Destroying Data Produced by Special Investigative Measures (SIM) from 28-30 June 2023 in Mavrovo. The need for a specific procedure was identified during multistakeholder workshops on the implementation of measures for the interception of communications that DCAF organised over the last two years. The development of a procedure on data destruction is also a recommendation from the Agency for Personal Data Protection as a safeguard for citizens’ privacy. During the workshop, the judicial ‘tight group’ discussed and identified the main aspects of the data destruction process for data produced by SIM, such as its legal basis and the responsible persons, steps, and deadlines for retaining and destroying data.

Between 5-7 June 2023 in Veles, DCAF organised a Workshop for MPs and Parliamentary Staff on “NATO and EU Approach to Security Sector Reform: Lessons for the Parliamentary Oversight”. The participants had an opportunity to get acquainted with NATO/EU standards and the obligations that NATO/EU membership entails through theoretical presentations, custom-made exercises, and expert facilitation. Participants increased their understanding of Parliamentarians’ requirements when exerting control and practicing oversight over the intelligence, security, and defense sector according to NATO/EU standards.

title.narrative: Indicator #2.3.1: Shielded Room and protected workspace constructed in Parliament and equipment installed.

comment.narrative: Baseline #2.3.1: The Parliament has no protected workspace and meeting facility to discuss and store classified information, impeding meaningful exchange of sensitive and classified information with security and intelligence services. Parliament, in Feb 2020, approved the establishment of the shielded room. Within its Phase I Programme DCAF allocated funds as a contribution towards the establishment of the Shielded Room and protected workplace. Due to Covid-19 the process was delayed throughout 2020.
Target #2.3.1: By the end of 2021 the Parliament has a Shielded Room and protected space Installed.

Between April and June 2023, DCAF organised several Workshops and Meetings on Developing Accreditation Documents for the Shielded Room and Protected Workspace in the Parliament of the Republic of North Macedonia. The workshops included stakeholders from across the intelligence and security sector institutions and were attended by four parliamentary staff from Security and Intelligence Committees, one IT staff member, representatives from the Directorate for Security of Classified Information, and representatives from the MoI responsible for the security of the Assembly and facilitated by a local expert. The workshops will continue until all accreditation documents are developed and deployed following the construction of the Shielded Room. The accreditation documents are essential to the use of the Shielded Room.The company for the construction of the Shielded Room has been selected by Parliament and construction is expected to begin in July and conclude in December 2023.

title.narrative: Indicator #2.5.1: Judicial practitioners receive training on judicial authorisation of SIM (more concretely on interception of communications), use of European legal standards and principles related to information collection.

comment.narrative: Baseline #2.5.1 - 2.5.3: No training delivered by the Academy on SIM
Target #2.5.2: Each year starting 2021 candidates for future judges and prosecutors selecting the subject on interception of communications, will undergo 9 academic classes.

On 09 June 2023, DCAF organised an Initial Meeting for the working group (WG) for the Development of a Collection of Case-Law on Special Investigative Measures (SIM) in North Macedonia. The Collection will serve as a training resource for the Academy for Judges and Public Prosecutors and is to be used in judicial courses at both entry- and higher-level education. It will complement the Benchbook, previously developed with DCAF’s support, and facilitate its application to local practice. The development process will provide an opportunity for the application of the European Convention on Human Rights to SIM authorisation in Macedonian proceedings and judicial reasoning to be analysed. This meeting centered around planning activities for the development of the Collection. DCAF will continue its support to the working group for the development of this knowledge product by sharing experiences and providing advice and mentorship. This will contribute to the Academy's ability to deliver academic classes on SIM.

title.narrative: Indicator #3.1.1: CSOs and Media report improved understanding of intelligence sector reforms, accountability requirements and police integrity.

comment.narrative: Baseline #3.1.1: CSOs and Media are not sufficiently equipped with knowledge and skills on intelligence sector reforms and accountability requirements, and police integrity to do monitoring and assessments of intelligence and law enforcement sector reforms.
Target #3.1.2: by 2023, 5 trainings/workshops delivered to CSOs and Media.

Between 26-28 April 2023 in Ohrid, DCAF organised a Multistakeholder Workshop on “Reconciling Parliamentary Oversight and Civilian Oversight over Intelligence and Security”. This was a joint workshop that brought together MPs and parliamentary staff of the three parliamentary committees supervising the intelligence and security sector and representatives of local CSOs and media (namely the CSO/media training group involved in the DCAF-led series of capacity building activities) in order to increase understanding of their different roles in ensuring a well-governed intelligence and security sector. Through tailored exercises and a scenario-based simulation, participants had the opportunity to enhance their knowledge of different forms of oversight in line with international human rights standards. In addition, the workshop served as a platform for trust building among oversight actors (Parliamentarians and CSOs/media) and, through a discussion of oversight functions and challenges, will contribute to better oversight practices.
Target #3.1.2: by 2023, 5 trainings/workshops delivered to CSOs and Media.

DCAF, as part of building capacity in CSOs and media organisations, organised Training no. 4 on Security Sector Governance and Accountability on the topic “NATO and EU Standards for Security Sector Reform: The Role of Democratic Oversight” from 01-03 June 2023. The training group, consisting of 14 representatives of local CSOs and media organisations, learned how to monitor security sector actor’s and institution’s compliance with NATO and EU standards through expert advice and tailor-made exercises. In addition, through integrated discussions, participants gained insight on the structure of NATO and the EU, the military aspects of security sector reform and the process of defense reform in North Macedonia, and justice and police reform processes in the context of Chapters 23 and 24 of the EU acquis.

title.narrative: Indicator #3.2.1: Public institutions legally mandated to oversee or control intelligence services report on their activities.

comment.narrative: Baseline #3.2.1: There is none or inconsistent public reporting by intelligence sector actors taking place.
Target #3.2.1: By 2022 four theoretical and practical trainings on report drafting organised with all intelligence sector actors.

Between 03-05 May 2023 in Mavrovo, DCAF held the Third Multi-stakeholder Workshop on Reporting Standards for Security/Intelligence Services and Control/Oversight Institutions. Representatives responsible for reporting, public relations, and inter-institutional cooperation from intelligence and security services and institutions with an oversight or control mandate attended the workshop. During the workshop, participants discussed reporting stages of development, identified common features in reports across institutions, and considered relevant standards for report writing and communication with the public. In addition, two CSO representatives presented the findings of their research on accountability and transparency in the Macedonian security and intelligence services which sparked interesting discussions on improving the services’ communication strategies. In the next period, a smaller group of selected participants will draft a document of common standards and principles for preparing public reports which will serve intelligence and security services/institutions as a guideline for better reporting to the relevant state institutions and the public.

title.narrative: Indicator #1.1 (a): Amended laws, bi-laws, and procedures on intelligence aligned with international principles, gender and human rights obligations, good practice and respecting the diversity of the citizens of the Republic of North Macedonia, adopted by Parliament.

comment.narrative: The current law, by-laws and procedures are not suitable to allow for effective oversight of the intelligence services. In addition, legally mandated oversight bodies are functioning but not sufficiently effective. The formal relationship between the Parliament and the Council for Civilian Supervision remains inadequate as a result.
By 2023 North Macedonia has suitable laws, by-laws and procedures (Law on Interception of Communications and other relevant laws;) allowing effective oversight over the intelligence services.

The draft Law on Amendments and Supplements to the Law on Interception of Communications is currently in Parliamentary procedure. It is expected to be voted on. The adoption of the Law would remove obstacles to the functioning of the Council for Civilian Supervision and enable technical experts to be hired for oversight. DCAF acted as a facilitator in the process, contributing to the law’s text and assisting to achieve political consensus.

title.narrative: OUTPUT 1.1. Security and Intelligence Institutions - Indicator #1.1.1: DCAF provides recommendations for any relevant intelligence sector legislation, including on gender and human rights obligations, as part of the legislative review process.
Guideline on Retention and Destruction of Data Collected by SIMs

comment.narrative: Current laws do not foster effective oversight. Enhanced legal authority and access to information are required to make oversight effective, in the Macedonian political context. The current law on AR, from 1996, does not sufficiently address increased requirements for intelligence accountability nor the new intelligence sector landscape, with OTA and the new law on intelligence coordination. No law on parliamentary oversight of intelligence exists, allowing for clear oversight powers, roles and effective oversight.
By 2025, DCAF has provided recommendations that respond to gaps in intelligence sector law and problems in implementation.

DCAF continues to strengthen intelligence institutions’ accountability and to provide recommendations and multistakeholder platforms leading to improved legislative frameworks in line with North Macedonia’s human rights obligations including gender equality. On 27 June 2025, DCAF supported the Operational-Technical Agency (OTA) in organizing multi-institutional roundtable discussion on Enhancing the Use of the Accredited System for Classified Information Exchange in Skopje. The discussion promoted regular and efficient use of the accredited secure system for the preparation and exchange of documentation between relevant stakeholders in the processes of initiating and approving proposals, requests and court orders for communications surveillance measures, endorsed by key speakers such as the OTA Director, the Minister of Interior, the Director of Public Security Bureau, and high level guests from the judiciary, intelligence and the military services. Attendees discussed the challenges that institutions are currently facing during the initial use of the system, proposed effective measures for enhanced inter-institutional connectivity and developed an Action plan with specific steps for efficient system use. DCAF will support OTA in monitoring the progress of the Action plan that should be fully implemented by the end of the year.

From 16-18 April in Ljubljana, the 1st Meeting of the Thematic Working Group on the Practical and Technical Implementation of the PCC Prüm Agreement - Automated Exchange of Dactyloscopic Data was held. Representatives from the Forensics Examinations Department – Dactyloscopy Unit attended the workshop. They presented the current status, latest developments, plans, and requirements in for achieving PCC Prüm operationalisation in the area of automated dactyloscopic data exchange. Their presentation included an overview of their respective department and information on the AFIS (automated fingerprints identification) system. Participants had the opportunity to learn about the technical preconditions for automated dactyloscopic data exchange and see its practical application (1st and 2nd step data exchange). Special attention was given to the evaluation procedure, with a walkthrough of the evaluation procedure for implementing the dactyloscopic data exchange provisions pursuant to the PCC Prüm Agreement. At the end of the meeting, evaluations of the non-EU PCC SEE Contracting Parties were conducted, and recommendations for next steps in becoming operational in the automated exchange of dactyloscopic data were provided. On 18 April, back-to-back with the previous meeting, the 3rd Meeting of the Thematic Working Group on the Practical and Technical Implementation of the PCC Prüm Agreement - Automated Exchange of DNA Data was organised. Representatives from the Forensics Examinations Department – DNA labs were invited and shared relevant developments and plans regarding the implementation of automated DNA data exchange in North Macedonia, as well as their current hit management at both national and international levels. This meeting provided a platform for all working group participants to raise and address any topics of interest, such as how colleagues overcome specific challenges encountered in daily work, aspects of automated DNA data exchange, and how other countries perform specific tasks in their work process.While the Ministry of Interior (MoI) of North Macedonia has already identified several missing requirements and a preliminary fact-finding assessment was supported by the DCAF-hosted PCC SEE Secretariat in early 2019, the MoI has since addressed some of the missing capacities.Following the meeting in Ljubljana, between 26-28 June, DCAF deployed an international expert to Skopje to conduct an on-site assessment of automated biometric dactyloscopy data processing and exchange. The expert assessed the Ministry’s state of play concerning the normative/legal, organisational, and technical aspects, providing a report with concrete recommendations for improving the capacities. It is crucial for North Macedonia to adopt a comprehensive approach to identify and address all missing capacities necessary for operational dactyloscopy data exchange in line with PCC Prüm Agreement. The MoI is expected to appoint a working group to prepare a strategy and action plan, periodically monitoring its implementation, and making appropriate adjustments. The assessment report will serve as the basis for this preparation. The international expert will remain available to advise the working group on addressing the identified gaps.

This initiative aims to align North Macedonia's criminal procedure with Euro-Atlantic standards, particularly in areas such as privacy, data retention, judicial oversight, proportionality, transparency, and accountability in the use of Special Investigative Measures (SIMs).

description.narrative: 2024 Report on the Realisation of the Action Plan for Implementing the Integrity Plan of the Ministry of Interior 2023-2025

comment.narrative: Over the last two years DCAF supported the MoI in the development and drafting of the Integrity Plan. Presently, the Integrity Plan is pending approval from the Minister of Interior. The Ministry of Interior (MoI) is amending the law on internal affairs to improve the internal control mechanisms that promote integrity. The new law will include integrity testing measures as a means of internal control, which will be applied to both current and future employees of the MoI. The MoI does not possess technical equipment to perform professional integrity testing, which will be a requirement in accordance to the new Law on Internal Affairs. In addition, the North Macedonian Police have revised their Code of Ethics in 2020.
By the end of 2025, 80% of DICCIPS employees report increasing their capacities for conducting criminal and disciplinary investigations.

In line with DCAF’s Programme priorities to strengthen internal control and prevent corruption within the Ministry of Interior (MoI), a high-level Roundtable on Police Integrity: Roles and Responsibilities of Police Managers was held on 5 March 2025. The event gathered Assistant Ministers and Heads of Sectors of Internal Affairs to discuss managerial responsibilities in promoting integrity and accountability. The roundtable highlighted the importance of leadership in fostering ethical conduct, sharing best practices, and advancing anti-corruption efforts. As the first event of its kind for mid- and senior-level MoI management, it set the foundation for an annual platform to support professional and ethical policing.
By the end of 2025, 80% of DICCIPS employees report increasing their capacities for conducting criminal and disciplinary investigations.

With DCAF’s support, the implementation of the Ministry of the Interior’s Integrity Plan 2023–2025 continues to advance. By providing strategic guidance and sustained assistance, DCAF played a key role in facilitating the implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of the plan. Following a DCAF-organized workshop held from 30 January to 1 February to assess the second year of implementation, the Internal Control Department released its second annual public report. This comprehensive report is available on the Ministry’s website in Macedonian, Albanian, and English. Looking ahead, the Internal Control Department remains committed to executing the 2025 Action Plan, with DCAF continuing to provide support in all phases of implementation, monitoring, and evaluation.

On 12 March 2025, DCAF launched a research initiative on judicial practices related to the authorisation and implementation of Special Investigative Measures (SIMs) in North Macedonia. Initiated at the request of the Academy of Judges and Public Prosecutors during Judicial Steering Group meetings, the initiative aims to enhance transparency and accountability in the use of SIMs. To support this effort, DCAF helped the Academy develop a comprehensive methodology of the research. This jointly agreed tool enables systematic analysis of judicial practices—both quantitative and qualitative—based on real case law and decisions. It also serves as a monitoring framework for ongoing evaluation of SIM authorisation and implementation.The research will be carried out by a working group comprising Academy representatives and members of the Judicial Group of Judges and Prosecutors. The research started with focus groups, which were held in Skopje on 24 and 25 March 2025 bringing together judges, prosecutors, Ministry of Interior officials, and legal experts to provide input and enrich the research with practical insights. As a next step of the research process, several workshops with the working group will be held to analyze the results from the interviews and the desktop research, review and compare the collected data, and conceptualize and draft the research report.
